experiment.description: Executable Python source only. No prose, Markdown or code fences. Use call(name, dict) and emit(value); responses are dictionaries.

uncertainties: Only integer lists of length 0-3 and values from {-10,-1,0,1,2,3,5,10} were tested.
Finite data cannot establish a universal law; other functions may coincide on these points.
Longer lists, larger magnitudes, and untested integers remain unverified.
interpretations.scope: Tested integer lists of length 0-3 with values in {-10,-1,0,1,2,3,5,10}, including empty, zero, duplicates, order swaps, and negatives.
interpretations.claim: For every observed input, evaluate returns the sum of squares of the input integers.

uncertainties: Only one swapped pair was tested.
Longer permutations and repeated elements in different positions remain untested.
interpretations.claim: On the tested pair, evaluate is order-insensitive.

uncertainties: Only singletons 0, 1, 2, and 5 were tested.
The empty-list behavior could be a special case rather than the empty sum.
interpretations.scope: Empty list and singleton inputs 0, 1, 2, and 5.
interpretations.claim: evaluate returns 0 for the empty list and n^2 for tested singleton inputs n.

uncertainties: Only -1 and -10 were tested as negative values.
Other negative integers and mixed-sign lists remain untested.
interpretations.scope: Two lists containing negative values: [-1,1] and [10,-10].
interpretations.claim: Negative inputs contribute positively, consistent with squaring rather than signed addition or product.

remaining_unknowns: Whether the sum-of-squares pattern holds for longer lists, larger magnitudes, and integer values not yet tested.
Whether the empty-list return 0 is the natural empty sum or a special case.
Whether any hidden order dependence appears for longer or repeated-element lists.
Whether the function is exactly sum of squares or another expression that coincides on the tested inputs.
Whether execution limits, overflow, or type handling alter results for large inputs.
review.suggested_next_question: Does evaluate([3,4]) return 25, as the sum-of-squares explanation predicts, or a different value that would falsify it?
